name: Mitani Seito Hane Sanuki Honpo (wasanbon, Higashikagawa)
ja: 三谷製糖羽根さぬき本舗
text: Wasanbon (fine-grained traditional Japanese sugar) maker in Higashikagawa, Kagawa, described as founded in Bunka 1 (1804). It works with sugar cane grown locally in Higashikagawa and makes the sugar by hand by craftsmen. Wasanbon is made in Kagawa and Tokushima; the Tokushima (Awa) tradition is said to have been spread about 220 years ago by an ascetic, Maruyama Tokuya of Kamiita, and to have won high regard in the late 18th century under domain protection.
flavor: Fine, melting wasanbon sugar; the sources give no tasting description beyond hand-made quality.
use: Sold as wasanbon for gifts and mail order; in a professional kitchen it is a fine-textured sweetener for wagashi and delicate sweets.
craft: Local cane and hand work are the points the maker emphasises. The sources reviewed do not describe the pressing, kneading (togi) or drying steps, so check these with the maker before specifying it.
src: Tabiiro Otoriyose, Mitani Seito Hane Sanuki Honpo

name: Yamaroku Shoyu (all-kioke shoyu, Shodoshima)
text: Shoyu brewery in Yasuda, Shodoshima, Kagawa, founded in the early Meiji era; the current president, Yamamoto Yasuo, is the fifth generation. Every shoyu is brewed in wooden kioke barrels, and the moromi building, more than 100 years old, is a nationally registered tangible cultural property. The president learned barrel making himself and runs a project to revive kioke craftsmen. Its shoyu is sold in about ten countries and regions.
flavor: Thick, mellow shoyu; press coverage describes it as dense and rounded.
use: Used as a finishing and table shoyu; the brewery is open to visitors from 9:00 to 17:00 year round, free of charge, no booking needed.
craft: Beams, earthen walls and floor of the old building are said to host diverse yeasts and lactic acid bacteria alongside the barrels, so the building is part of the process. The sources do not give koji ratios or ageing times.
src: Ryori Tsushin, kioke craftsman revival project

name: Honke Matsuura Shuzojo (Narutotai, Naruto)
text: Sake brewery in Naruto, Tokushima, founded in Bunka 1 (1804) by the second-generation Matsuura Naozo Yoshiyu. The brand Narutotai was approved as a registered trademark in 1886 (Meiji 19). It stands on the Muya Kaido, once a busy approach to the Shikoku pilgrimage, and is described as the oldest surviving sake brewery in Tokushima. The Chugoku-Shikoku agricultural bureau of MAFF has profiled its sake exports.
flavor: Not described in the sources reviewed beyond the Narutotai brand.
use: Brand sold domestically and exported; MAFF highlights export of Tokushima sake overseas.
craft: The sources reviewed give dates and export activity but no detail of rice, yeast or brewing method; confirm specifications with the brewery.

name: Kondo Shuzo (Ehime sake brewery)
text: Ehime sake brewery listed as founded in 1878. According to a regional brewery guide it stopped brewing for a period and resumed around 2000, which makes it a revived rather than continuous house. The guide gives no town or process detail in the passage seen.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Local sake; see the Ehime brewery guide for brands.
craft: Check the brewery directly: the source seen records only the founding year and the closure and revival, not rice, yeast or equipment.

name: Umebijin Shuzo (Ehime, chimney brewery)
text: Ehime sake brewery known for a large chimney from its 1928 building, which is a nationally registered tangible cultural property. The brewery guide cites the architecture as its symbol; details of rice and method are not given in the passage seen.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.

name: Hamayoshiya (katsuobushi, Usa, Tosa)
text: Katsuobushi maker in Usa, Tosa city, Kochi. Its own account says it began in the early Meiji period (around the Restoration), when Harimaya Kamezo, a man from Kishu (Wakayama), taught the katsuobushi method locally. Over time the house added methods of its own suited to the Tosa climate.
flavor: Not described in the search summary; see the maker's page.
use: Katsuobushi for dashi; Usa is a long-standing Tosa bonito port.
craft: The lineage runs from Kishu technique adapted to Tosa's climate. The sources seen do not detail smoking, mould-ageing cycles or grades; ask the maker for specifications.

name: Takemasa Shoten (soda-bushi, Tosashimizu)
text: Katsuobushi house in Tosashimizu, Kochi, founded in Taisho 1 (1912). At first it also made dried sardines, tengusa, kamaboko and salt. It later gave up operating its own bonito boats and concentrated on katsuobushi alone. Its own account says Tosashimizu production is mainly soda-bushi (from frigate or bullet mackerel, soda-gatsuo).
flavor: Not described in the source seen; soda-bushi is generally a strong, fatty dashi material.
use: Soda-bushi and related katsuobushi for dashi; the maker sells directly.
craft: The house shifted from mixed marine processing to single-product specialisation. The source seen has no details of smoking or shaving grades.

name: Yoshinaga Katsuobushi-ten (straw-grilled katsuo tataki, Kochi)
text: Kochi katsuobushi shop presented by a Kochi Bank regional blog as having more than 90 years of history. It is known for warazaki-yaki katsuo no tataki, bonito seared over burning rice straw in the Tosa manner. The blog does not give the exact founding year, so the age is as of the blog's writing.
flavor: Straw-fired bonito; the blog describes it as an outstanding tataki.
use: Straw-seared bonito tataki sold by the shop.
craft: The distinguishing technique is straw (wara) firing rather than gas; the blog gives no times or temperatures.

name: Tsukasabotan Shuzo (Kochi)
text: Kochi sake brewery presented by a Kochi tourism page as a house with more than four hundred years of history (the page words it as over 410 years). The summary seen gives no town, rice or technique detail.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Tosa sake, usually paired in Kochi with bonito and local seafood.
craft: The only claim in the source seen is the long history; the figure is the tourism page's wording and was not checked against the brewery's own record.

text: Sake brewery in Tano town, Aki district, eastern Kochi, listed as founded in 1903. It is one of a group of small eastern Kochi breweries named in a Tosa breweries guide alongside Arimitsu Shuzojo and Sentou Shuzojo.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.

name: Arimitsu Shuzojo (Aki, Kochi)

name: Kochi Shuzo (merged brewery, Ino)
text: Sake company in Ino town, Kochi, set up in 1944 when 28 brewers in the prefecture were merged under wartime consolidation. According to the guide seen, it still operates as a joint structure of 22 companies. It is a rare example of a wartime amalgamation that remains a shared brewery.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Prefectural sake brewed for several member houses.
craft: The figures (28 merged in 1944, 22 now) come from a regional guide; check current membership with the company.

name: Yamauchi Honten (Kumamoto miso and shoyu)
text: Kumamoto miso, shoyu and koji maker whose own site gives its founding as Horeki 1 (1751). It stresses koji and uses subsurface water from the Aso outer rim as brewing water. It also runs a koji-focused sideline, Hibi Koujiya.
flavor: Kyushu-style sweeter miso and shoyu are typical of the region; the maker's page emphasises koji character.
use: Miso, shoyu and koji seasonings for home and kitchen use.
craft: Aso outer-rim water and in-house koji are the stated points; the sources seen do not give koji ratios or ageing times.

name: Fundodai (Kumamoto shoyu and miso)
text: Kumamoto shoyu and miso maker founded in Ansei 6 (1859). A Kyushu tourism feature lists it among eight notable Kyushu shoyu. It brews from its own koji to moromi at its own brewery, using wheat grown in Oita among its raw materials.
flavor: Kyushu-style rounded, sweeter shoyu, per the regional feature; no more specific description in the source.
use: Table and cooking shoyu for Kyushu dishes.
craft: In-house koji making and moromi are the points given; the pages seen do not specify barrel type or ageing time.

name: Fundokin Shoyu (Oita)
text: Oita miso and shoyu maker founded in Bunkyu 1 (1861); a Kyushu tourism feature says it reaches its 165th anniversary in 2026. It is one of the large regional houses featured among Kyushu shoyu makers.
flavor: Sweet-leaning Kyushu style, per regional description.
use: Shoyu and miso for home and food service.
craft: The source seen gives dates only; production methods and scale were not stated.

name: Hita Shoyu (Hita, Oita)
text: Miso and shoyu brewer in Hita, Oita, whose shop site claims 170 years of traditional method and the honour of supplying the Emperor. The founding year is not stated in the passage seen, so the 170 years is the company's own wording.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Premium miso and shoyu sold by mail order.
craft: The royal-supply claim and age are self-reported; no process details were retrievable.

name: Naganomo Miso Shoyu Jozomoto (Miyazaki)
text: Miyazaki brewery founded in 1877 in Miyazaki city, making mugi (barley) miso and sweet shoyu with its own koji by older methods. A NIHONMONO feature describes it as carrying southern Kyushu flavours abroad.
flavor: Sweet barley miso and sweet shoyu, typical of Miyazaki.
use: Mugi miso for soups and dengaku, sweet shoyu for sashimi and simmering in Kyushu style.
craft: Self-made koji and traditional methods are the stated points; no ratios or ageing times in the source seen.

name: Kamimura Shuzo (Okinawa awamori)
text: Okinawan awamori distillery stated to have been founded in Meiji 15 (1882). Its brands include Danryu and Shurei. The site presents it as a distillery with more than a century of history.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Awamori for drinking neat, on the rocks or diluted with water.
craft: The source gives founding year and brand names only; ask the distillery about koji, still type and ageing in kame.

name: Masahiro Shuzo (Shuri awamori)
text: Awamori distillery stated to have been founded in Meiji 16 (1883) in Shuri. The founder, Higa Masafumi, was a son of Higa Masatsugu, who had been head chef in the Ryukyu court.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.

The founder, Kawada Wasuke, started as the Kawada Jozoten. The company names wooden-barrel stills (kidaru jyoryuki) and rice koji among its methods.

name: Nishimura Asamori Shoten (Makurazaki katsuobushi)
text: Katsuobushi maker in Makurazaki, Kagoshima, founded in 1950 and twice winner of the Minister of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries Prize. Makurazaki is Japan's honkarebushi centre, where mould (kabi-tsuke) was added in the Meiji era after the technique had come from Kishu around 300 years earlier.
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Honkarebushi for dashi.
craft: Awards and Makurazaki origin are documented; kabi-tsuke rounds and grade details are not given. A Makurazaki honkarebushi was certified as authentic by the local association.

name: Ageson Katsuobushi-ten (Makurazaki)
text: Makurazaki katsuobushi maker founded in 1930 (Showa 5) when the first-generation owner went independent; now run by the fourth generation. It is described in an article on Makurazaki's katsuobushi history, in which one date given for the technique's arrival is Hoei 4 (1707).
flavor: Not described in the source seen.
use: Katsuobushi for dashi.
craft: The article credits a Kishu origin for the technique; sources conflict slightly on how the date is stated (1707 versus 'about 300 years').

name: Fukuchiyo Shuzo (Nabeshima, Kashima)
text: Small sake brewery of about 400 koku a year in the Hizen-hama-juku area of Kashima, Saga, facing the Ariake Sea. Founded in the late Taisho era; its name Fukuchiyo dates from wartime enterprise consolidation. The brand Nabeshima was launched in 1998 after three years of planning, named by public contest with permission from Nabeshima family descendants. It won IWC Champion Sake in 2011. Brewer-owner Iimori Naoki helped start Kashima Sake Brewery Tourism.
flavor: Full, soft rice sweetness with a fresh effervescent quality in the shiboritate styles, per brewery profiles.
use: Sake brand sold nationally and abroad after the 2011 IWC award.
craft: The brewery stresses individual character per product over mass production. Sources seen give no rice, polish or yeast specification.

name: Castella Honke Fukusaya (Nagasaki)
text: Nagasaki castella maker founded in Kan'ei 1 (1624), according to Wikipedia, as a house handling sugar and rice before becoming a castella specialist. Castella is the Portuguese-origin sponge cake of Nagasaki; the house is regarded as one of the three major castella makers. Sources describe hand-made production.
flavor: Rich egg sponge with a moist crumb and sugar crystals on the base, typical of Nagasaki castella.
use: Gift sweet; sliced and eaten with tea.
craft: Hand-making is the emphasis. Founding is given as 1624 by Wikipedia; no process measures in the sources.

name: Shooken (Nagasaki castella)

flavor: Not described precisely in the source seen.
use: Castella gift cake, sliced.
